claims.text: The candidate material is an Al-containing refractory high-entropy alloy similar in composition to Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr.
The candidate alloy initially has a predominantly disordered BCC matrix.
The initial alloy exhibits stable ductility over a broad temperature range.
Intermediate-temperature aging at approximately 400–500 °C for tens of hours induces partial ordering and formation of a B2-like phase.
A higher-temperature solutionizing treatment reverses the ordering and dissolves the B2-like phase.
Homogenization produces a ductile disordered phase at room temperature.
An ordered B2 phase is more embrittling than a continuous BCC matrix in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Intermediate-temperature aging transiently reduces ductility by producing B2 ordering within the disordered matrix.
Dissolution of the ordered B2 phase restores a ductile disordered BCC structure.
Ductility decreases significantly as the B2 fraction increases.
Aging creates a narrow brittle phase field between initially ductile and subsequently restored ductile states.
Solutionizing after aging recovers ductility and completes a ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
The untreated alloy has high ductility without a pronounced brittle window.
The transition depends on precise aging temperatures and durations that control the ordered-phase fraction.
Processing outside the proposed temperature and time windows may cause incomplete phase transformation or degradation of other mechanical properties.
The kinetics of B2 formation and dissolution, the critical brittle-phase fraction, and cycle reproducibility are not fully determined.
